title: Amitabha
hook: Buddha of Infinite Light and Infinite Life

segments.voice: Yesterday, the primal vow: entrusting, wishing, the name, and a door the sutra says is already open. Your line was the primal vow. What unearned door did you notice? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-eight.

A gilded figure seated on a temple altar in Japan, hands resting in the lap, fingers and thumbs forming two small circles. A tall standing figure in a Chinese hall, one hand raised, the other lowered and open, as if reaching down to someone. A small paper image taped above a bed in a nursing home. Three images, one Buddha. In Japan he is Amida. In China, Amituofo. In the Sanskrit sutras, he carries two names, and today's word is the first of them: Amitabha.
screen: `A SEATED FIGURE IN JAPAN.` → `A HAND REACHING DOWN.` → `AMITABHA.`

segments.voice: First, the two names, and the sutra explains them itself. In the short sutra on the land of bliss, the Buddha asks Shariputra: why is that Buddha called Amitabha? Because his light is measureless, and shines without obstruction over the Buddha-lands in every direction. And why is he also called Amitayus? Because his life, and the life of the people in his land, is measureless too. Amitabha, infinite light. Amitayus, infinite life. The Japanese name Amida holds both. Second, who he is. He is the monk from two days ago. The longer sutra says Dharmakara kept his vows, became a Buddha, and lives now in the land of bliss. So every time someone says his name, they are naming a vow kept. Third, the light itself. Notice what the sutra says about it: without obstruction. Sunlight on a city doesn't pick which roofs to land on. In the sutra, Amitabha's light behaves the same way. It reaches every land, near and far. And one clarification, since the shops confuse it. Amitabha is not the laughing, round-bellied figure sold in gift shops. That is Budai, Hotei in Japan, a different figure altogether. Fourth, how people meet him. Through images like the ones at the start. Through the name, said in Japanese, Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese. And, the short sutra says, at the end of life: when a person who has held his name in mind is dying, Amitabha appears before them with a holy company. Some readers see that welcome in the lowered hand of the standing statue, reaching down.
screen: `TWO NAMES: LIGHT AND LIFE.` · `DHARMAKARA, A VOW KEPT.` · `LIGHT WITHOUT OBSTRUCTION.` · `THE HAND REACHING DOWN.` · then, large: `INFINITE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Close your eyes. Picture a small, warm light in the center of your chest, about the size of a candle flame. With each out-breath, let it grow. It fills your body. Then the room. Then the building, the street, the city. Let it keep spreading until it has no edge at all, and nothing blocks it: not walls, not distance, not anyone's past. Rest in that boundless light, breathing. The bell holds the time.
Amitabha. The Buddha of infinite light, also called Amitayus, infinite life: Amida in Japan, Amituofo in China, the monk Dharmakara with his vows fulfilled. Today's word.
Your line: infinite light. Today, when you see sunlight fall on a street, notice that it doesn't choose which roofs or which faces to light. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists keep images of Amitabha, seated or standing with one hand lowered in welcome, on temple and home altars, and call his name as Namu Amida Butsu in Japan or Namo Amituofo in China.

fork.setup: you're Shariputra, and the Buddha asks you why that Buddha is called Amitabha. what's the sutra's answer?
options: because his land lies in the west.
because his light is measureless and shines without obstruction.
because he was once a king.
fork.reveal: the short sutra gives the reason itself: measureless light, unobstructed in every direction. measureless life gives him his second name, Amitayus.

original.note: Sanskrit: Amitabha, infinite light. his second name, Amitayus (अमितायुस्), means infinite life. Japanese Amida (阿弥陀).

trapdoor: what you thought: a statue of the Buddha.
what it means: the Buddha of infinite light and life, who was once the monk Dharmakara.
what a scholar hears: two Sanskrit names, Amitabha and Amitayus, held together in the one Japanese name Amida.

sources.ref: Smaller Sukhavati-vyuha (why he is called Amitabha and Amitayus; his appearing at the end of life)

notes: The two names are explained from the Smaller Sukhavati-vyuha's own words (paraphrased); in some versions of the sutra both explanations appear under the name Amitayus/Amitabha in slightly different order. Confirm.
Image descriptions (seated figure with meditation mudra; standing figure with one hand lowered) are general; confirm the lowered hand as a gesture of welcome (raigo).
Budai/Hotei distinction: confirm wording is respectful to both.
Japanese Amida (阿弥陀) and Sanskrit Amitayus spelling in Devanagari (अमितायुस्): confirm.
Deathbed welcome mentioned briefly; day 1270 covers end-of-life practice.
Editor: the link between the deathbed welcome and the standing statue's lowered hand is now 'some readers see', since the sutra does not describe statues.
